topic: PE Epidemiology and Virchow's Triad
content: Pulmonary embolism: blood clot obstructing pulmonary arteries. Incidence 60-100 per 100,000 annually. Mortality 2-10% treated, 30% untreated. Virchow's triad: venous stasis (immobility, obesity, surgery), endothelial injury (trauma, central lines, atrial fibrillation), hypercoagulability (malignancy, thrombophilia, estrogen). Risk stratification: massive (hemodynamic instability, RV strain), submassive (RV strain but stable), stable (no RV strain).

topic: Wells Score for PE Clinical Probability
content: Wells score (0-12.5 points): predicts pretest probability PE. Points: PE most likely diagnosis (3), heart rate >100 (1.5), signs of DVT (3), hemoptysis (1), signs of shock (3.5 if hypotensive, 1.5 if syncope), atelectasis/consolidation not lateral (1.5), CXR normal (1.5). Score <2: low risk (1.3% PE). 2-6: moderate risk (16.2% PE). >6: high risk (37.5% PE). If low clinical probability + normal D-dimer: PE ruled out. Used in two-level PE-protocol (Wells + D-dimer).

topic: D-Dimer Interpretation and Clinical Context
content: D-dimer: marker of thrombin generation/fibrin degradation (high sensitivity, low specificity). Normal D-dimer (<500 ng/mL) has 95-99% negative predictive value for VTE in low-to-moderate pretest probability. Elevated in: PE, DVT, MI, sepsis, DIC, trauma, cancer, pregnancy, postoperative state. Not useful to rule in PE (elevated in many conditions). Age-adjusted cutoff (age × 10 ng/mL) improves specificity in elderly. High D-dimer doesn't require imaging if low clinical suspicion.

topic: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) - Interpretation
content: CTPA: gold standard for PE diagnosis. Findings: main pulmonary artery (massive PE), lobar (large emboli), segmental (moderate), subsegmental (small, controversial significance). Sensitivity 94-98%, specificity 95-98%. Can detect alternative diagnoses (pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, aortic dissection). Subsegmental PE (SSPE): clinical significance debated; isolated SSPE in hemodynamically stable patient may not require anticoagulation (NEJM 2024). Right heart strain on CT (RV/LV ratio >0.9) prognostically important.

topic: PE - Clinical Presentation and Red Flags
content: PE presentation: dyspnea (73%), chest pain (52%, often pleuritic), syncope (5%, often massive PE), sudden cardiac arrest (2%, fulminant). Tachycardia, tachypnea common. S1Q3T3 on ECG (classic but rare, 10-15%), more commonly sinus tachycardia/NSR with nonspecific changes. Calf swelling/pain suggests DVT source. Absence of dyspnea doesn't rule out PE; maintain high suspicion. Signs of RV strain/shock indicate massive PE.

topic: PE - ECG Findings and Troponin/BNP
content: ECG: S1Q3T3 (>10% cases), sinus tachycardia, right axis deviation, RV strain pattern (T wave inversion V1-V3, sometimes others). New AFib possible. ECG normal doesn't exclude PE. Troponin elevation: present in 30-50% PE, indicates RV injury, worse prognosis. BNP elevation: indicates RV strain, prognostically important. Neither troponin nor BNP diagnostic for PE; used for risk stratification in confirmed PE (prognostic).

topic: Echocardiography in PE - RV Strain Assessment
content: Echocardiography findings in PE: RV dilatation (RV/LV ratio >0.9), RV dysfunction (reduced RV systolic strain), elevated pulmonary artery pressure (TR velocity >2.8 m/s = PA systolic >35), McConnell's sign (RV free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing, specific for PE). Echo useful to identify RV dysfunction (prognostic), assess for alternative diagnoses (tamponade, perioperative MI), right heart catheterization not routinely needed. Normal echo doesn't exclude PE (may be normal in subsegmental PE).

topic: Massive PE vs Submassive PE vs Stable PE
content: Massive PE: systemic hypotension (SBP <90 for >15 min) or shock (lactate >2, oliguria, altered mental status), high mortality 30-50%. Requires thrombolysis or embolectomy. Submassive PE: hemodynamically stable but with RV dysfunction (echo findings, elevated troponin/BNP), mortality 5-10%, intermediate therapy considered. Stable PE: no RV dysfunction, normal troponin/BNP, mortality <5%, anticoagulation alone sufficient. Risk stratification guides therapy (anticoagulation vs thrombolysis vs mechanical intervention).

topic: V/Q Scanning - Limited Modern Use
content: Ventilation-perfusion scans: historically used for PE diagnosis, largely replaced by CTPA. Still used if: contrast allergy, renal insufficiency, pregnancy (lower radiation/iodine exposure). Findings: normal (PE excluded), low probability, intermediate probability (inconclusive), high probability. Low + low clinical suspicion = PE excluded. High + high clinical suspicion = PE confirmed. Intermediate results + discordant clinical probability = need CTPA or D-dimer.

topic: PE Screening in Asymptomatic Patients - When to Consider
content: Screening for asymptomatic PE (incidental pulmonary emboli) controversial. Found on 1-2% of CT angiographies for other indications. Most isolated subsegmental PEs in asymptomatic patients don't require anticoagulation (low bleeding risk outweighs benefit). Treatment depends: main/lobar PE = anticoagulate even if asymptomatic; segmental = consider clinical context (cancer, hypercoagulable state); subsegmental = usually observe. High clinical judgment needed; avoid reflexively treating incidental PE.

topic: PE in Special Populations - Pregnancy
content: PE in pregnancy: increased risk (especially third trimester/postpartum), mortality higher. Dyspnea/tachycardia harder to distinguish from normal pregnancy. Imaging: CTPA relatively safe (fetal radiation <1 rad); V/Q scan alternative if contrast allergy (higher fetal risk than CTPA). Anticoagulation: LMWH preferred (doesn't cross placenta), UFH also safe. Warfarin avoided (teratogenic first trimester, fetal hemorrhage risk). Thrombolysis reserved for massive PE (maternal mortality >25%). IVC filter if anticoagulation contraindicated.

topic: DVT Epidemiology and Risk Factors
content: Deep vein thrombosis: clot in leg veins (popliteal, femoral, iliac). Incidence 1-2 per 1000 annually. Risk: immobilization (surgery, paralysis), malignancy, thrombophilia, recent surgery/trauma, central lines, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, hormone therapy. Virchow's triad applies. Complications: pulmonary embolism (10-50% untreated), post-thrombotic syndrome (20-50%), recurrent thrombosis if untreated.

topic: Wells Score for DVT Clinical Probability
content: Wells score DVT (0-8 points): clinical suspicion before ultrasound. Points: active cancer (1), leg immobilization (1), recent surgery requiring general anesthesia (1), calf swelling >3cm vs other (1), pitting edema unilateral (1), collateral superficial veins (1), entire leg swelling (1), localized tenderness along deep veins (1), alternative diagnosis likely (-2). Score 0-1: low risk (5% DVT). 2-6: moderate risk (17% DVT). >6: high risk (53% DVT). Very low score + normal D-dimer = DVT excluded.

topic: Compression Ultrasound - DVT Diagnosis Gold Standard
content: Compression ultrasound: gold standard for DVT diagnosis. Sensitivity/specificity >95%. Technique: apply probe pressure (compress veins); thrombus = vein doesn't collapse completely. Exam limited if: severe edema, bandages, pain, obesity (operator-dependent). Proximal DVT (popliteal, femoral, iliac): single abnormal US diagnostic. Distal DVT (calf veins): if negative, repeat in 5-7 days if high suspicion (20% propagate proximally). MRI/CT if ultrasound inconclusive or IVC suspected involved.

topic: DVT Presentation and Physical Examination
content: DVT presentation: unilateral leg edema/swelling (most common), calf pain/tenderness, erythema, warmth. Homan's sign (calf pain with dorsiflexion) and Pratt's sign (adductor tenderness) not specific. Phlegmasia: severe DVT with compromised venous return, cyanosis, severe pain, skin necrosis (emergency). Bilateral swelling: suggests IVC involvement or medical causes (heart failure, renal disease). Absence of symptoms doesn't exclude DVT (20% asymptomatic in hospitalized patients).

topic: Superficial Thrombophlebitis vs DVT
content: Superficial venous thrombosis (SVT): clot in superficial veins (saphenous, tributaries). Presents with cord-like tenderness, erythema, pain along vein path. Lower risk of PE (1-3%) vs DVT. Management: anticoagulation if: >5cm from saphenofemoral junction, involves saphenofemoral junction, concurrent DVT, malignancy, thrombophilia. Otherwise: NSAIDs, compression, early mobilization may suffice. Duplex ultrasound confirms diagnosis and assesses proximity to deep system. Repeat US in 1 week if SVT extends toward saphenofemoral junction.

topic: IVC Thrombosis - Special Consideration
content: Inferior vena cava (IVC) thrombosis: rare but serious, risk of massive PE, bilaterally compromised perfusion. Causes: IVC filter, malignancy invading IVC, primary thrombosis (thrombophilia), hypercoagulable state. Presentation: bilateral leg edema, dilated superficial veins (collateral), pain. Diagnosis: CT with contrast or duplex ultrasound of IVC. Management: anticoagulation (UFH preferred if IVC filter removal needed), consider thrombolysis if massive. Prognosis: depends on extent, cause; recurrence risk high without addressing underlying cause.

topic: VTE Risk Stratification for Anticoagulation Duration
content: Provoked DVT (surgery, immobilization, cancer, trauma): anticoagulation 3 months if reversible risk, longer (6-12 months) if malignancy. Unprovoked DVT (no clear precipitant): anticoagulation ≥3 months; extended therapy (indefinite) if recurrent VTE, cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, thrombophilia, or inadequate anticoagulation. D-dimer after stopping anticoagulation: if positive, increased recurrence risk (guides extended therapy decision). Male sex, proximal DVT, RV dysfunction, elevated D-dimer suggest higher recurrence risk.

topic: Anticoagulation Agents - LMWH vs UFH vs DOAC
content: LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h): outpatient treatment, predictable pharmacokinetics, no monitoring required, good for most patients. UFH IV (80 units/kg bolus, then infusion 18 units/kg/hr): inpatient, used if renal failure (CrCl <30), need for rapid reversal, or embolectomy planned. DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran): oral, avoid if severe renal disease, pregnancy, malignancy (concern DOAC vs warfarin). Initial parenteral anticoagulation (LMWH/UFH) bridge 5-7 days for warfarin; DOACs can start immediately. All effective; choice based on renal function, pregnancy status, bleeding risk.

topic: Warfarin vs DOAC - Indications and Drug Interactions
content: Warfarin: vitamin K antagonist, slower onset (5-7 days), requires INR monitoring (goal 2-3 for VTE), multiple drug interactions, food interactions (vitamin K). Advantages: reversible (vitamin K, FFP), cheap long-term. Disadvantages: lots of monitoring, food/drug interactions. DOACs: faster onset, no monitoring, fewer interactions (apixaban/dabigatran least). Advantages: convenience, no monitoring. Disadvantages: not reversible (though reversal agents available), expensive initially, avoid if CrCl <15-30 depending on agent, not for cancer thrombosis. Choice: patient preference, renal function, drug interactions, ability to monitor (warfarin).

topic: IVC Filter Indications and Complications
content: IVC filter: mechanical barrier to prevent PE in anticoagulation contraindicated/failing patients. Indications: absolute = acute PE + anticoagulation contraindicated (active bleeding, HIT); relative = proximal DVT + high bleeding risk, unable to anticoagulate. Complications: filter thrombosis, IVC stenosis, migration, perforation (rare, usually benign), difficult retrieval if retrievable filter left in too long. Retrievable filters should be removed within 3 months (permanent filters reserved for expected lifelong contraindication). Anticoagulation should still be used when safe; filter is bridge only.

topic: Post-Thrombotic Syndrome (PTS) - Prevention and Management
content: Post-thrombotic syndrome: chronic venous insufficiency (20-50% after DVT) presenting with leg swelling, pain, skin changes, ulceration. Risk: proximal DVT >distal, incomplete thrombus resolution, inadequate anticoagulation. Prevention: early anticoagulation, leg elevation, compression stockings (class 2-3, 30-40 mmHg for 2 years post-DVT shows benefit in some trials). Management: compression therapy, leg elevation, exercise, skin care, vein surgery if severe/ulceration. CEAP classification grades severity. No specific pharmacotherapy proven effective.

topic: Bleeding Risk in VTE Anticoagulation - HAS-BLED Score
content: HAS-BLED score predicts major bleeding risk during anticoagulation: hypertension (1), abnormal renal/liver function (1 each), stroke (1), bleeding history (1), labile INR (1), elderly (>65, 1), drugs/alcohol (1 each). Score 0-1: low risk (<2% annual bleeding). 2-3: moderate risk. >3: high risk. VTE anticoagulation benefit usually outweighs bleeding risk; need shared decision-making in high-risk patients. Strategies to reduce bleeding: shorter initial anticoagulation, use DOAC if possible (more predictable than warfarin), PPI for GI bleed prevention if history, avoid NSAIDs.

topic: Reversal of Anticoagulation - Warfarin, DOAC, Heparin
content: Warfarin reversal: vitamin K 10mg IV slow (onset 12-24h, persistent reversal), FFP 10-15 mL/kg (immediate but temporary, volume overload risk), prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC, 25 units/kg, preferred for urgent reversal). DOAC reversal: idarucizumab (dabigatran antidote), apixaban/rivaroxaban (activated factor X - andexanet alfa expensive/limited availability). Heparin reversal: protamine 1 mg per 100 units UFH (IV over 10 min, max 50 mg per dose). Reversal needs urgent evaluation by hematology if major bleeding.

topic: Thrombophilia Workup - When and How
content: Thrombophilia testing indicated: unprovoked VTE, VTE age <40, recurrent VTE, VTE with family history, mesenteric/portal venous thrombosis. Tests: Factor V Leiden (most common, 5% Caucasians), prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin deficiency, protein C/S deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome (anticardiolipin, beta-2 glycoprotein, lupus anticoagulant). Timing: test during anticoagulation (warfarin doesn't affect most), but avoid acute phase (elevated D-dimer, decreased protein S). Results guide extended anticoagulation decision if positive. Heterozygous Factor V Leiden = low recurrence risk; homozygous/multiple mutations = higher risk.

topic: Cancer and VTE - DOAC vs Warfarin Controversy
content: Cancer-associated VTE: 5-7% of cancer patients develop VTE; associated with poor outcomes. Historically warfarin preferred (DOACs not studied adequately in cancer trials). Recent trials (HOKUSAI-VTE-C, SELECT-D): DOAC (edoxaban, apixaban) non-inferior/superior to warfarin in cancer VTE. Practice evolving: DOACs now reasonable option for cancer VTE if not GI cancer or significant drug interactions. LMWH still reasonable if DOAC unavailable/contraindicated, or bridging. Duration: indefinite for active cancer; can discontinue after cancer remission (similar to non-cancer VTE). Inferior vena cava filter consideration if anticoagulation contraindicated.

topic: Recurrent VTE - Workup and Prolonged Anticoagulation
content: Recurrent VTE: first episode treated 3 months, then evaluate for extended therapy. Second unprovoked VTE: indefinite anticoagulation usually recommended. Workup for recurrent despite anticoagulation: compliance check, efficacy of chosen agent (ensure therapeutic levels), occult malignancy (cancer screening if not recently done), thrombophilia, antiphospholipid syndrome, recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis. D-dimer guidance: persistently elevated post-anticoagulation = higher recurrence risk (favors extended anticoagulation). Extended anticoagulation (indefinite) reduces recurrence 80-85% vs stopping anticoagulation.

topic: PERT (PE Response Teams) - Multidisciplinary Approach
content: PE Response Teams (PERT): multidisciplinary team (pulmonary, cardiology, interventional radiology, critical care, anticoagulation specialist) for risk stratification and management decisions in PE. Benefits: reduce time to intervention, improve risk stratification, increase thrombolysis use in appropriate candidates, reduce mortality (some studies). Available at larger medical centers. Useful for: massive PE, submassive with hemodynamic compromise, uncertainty about anticoagulation vs thrombolysis, complicated cases. Coordinated care improves outcomes vs isolated specialist recommendations.

topic: VTE Prophylaxis - Medical and Surgical Patients
content: VTE prophylaxis in hospitalized patients: anticoagulation (LMWH, fondaparinux, warfarin) or mechanical (compression devices, sequential compression stockings, early mobilization). Medical patients: risk assessment (Padua score, IMPROVE score); moderate-high risk = VTE prophylaxis. Surgical patients: type-specific prophylaxis (general surgery = LMWH 12 days; orthopedic = extended LMWH ±warfarin 10-35 days). Duration: continues until discharge or risk resolved. Contraindications: active bleeding, recent ICH, thrombocytopenia <50k, HIT. Mechanical prophylaxis alone if anticoagulation contraindicated.

topic: Pulmonary Hypertension Post-PE - Chronic Thromboembolic PH
content: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH): occurs if PE clots not completely resolved, leading to chronic RV strain, dyspnea, RV failure. Incidence 0.1-4% after acute PE. Risk: large PE, recurrent PE, inadequate anticoagulation. Diagnosis: right heart catheterization (elevated mean PA pressure >25 mmHg at rest), CT angiography (mosaic perfusion, webs/bands), ventilation-perfusion scan (mismatched defects). Management: lifelong anticoagulation, pulmonary vasodilators (ambrisentan, bosentan, sildenafil), pulmonary endarterectomy if operable (curative, 5-10 year survival benefit). Early recognition/referral critical.
